title: Head shakes, feet stagger
hookLine: the head shakes, the feet stagger, the eyes grow dim; still you don't turn (Salok M9, ang 1428)

lines: IT NEVER SAYS NO, ONLY LATER.
LATER, PAINTED IN A FEW STROKES.
cards: Here's a someday list. Someday I'll call my brother and make peace. Someday I'll learn to read Gurmukhi properly.
Someday, when the kids are older, when work calms down, when I retire. The list is kind to us. It never says no.
It just says later. And later has a way of turning into a doctor's waiting room, a walker by the door, glasses that don't quite help.
Guru Tegh Bahadur's salok paints that later in a few quick strokes, and then asks a question that stings.

teach.b: The salok says sir kampio pag dagmage, nain jot te heen. In paraphrase: the head shakes, the feet stagger, the eyes have lost their light.
Says Nanak, this is what has happened, and still the mind isn't absorbed in the Lord's love. Sir is the head; kampio, it trembles.
Pag dagmage, the feet totter. Nain jot te heen, the eyes without their light. A portrait of great age, in three short strokes.
But it's easy to hear it wrong. The salok is not mocking old people. The body's weakness isn't the problem in the line at all.
The problem is the last half: tau na har ras leen, still not absorbed in the Lord's sweetness.
The body has been sending signals for years, and the mind has kept saying later. So the salok isn't about the elderly. It's about the someday list, held by people of every age.
And it's one reason Sikh families honor their elders. Some of them did turn while they could.
They're the ones who taught grandchildren the Mool Mantar, who kept the morning prayers when no one else was awake, whose shaking hands still fold for Ardas.
A Sikh elder at the gurdwara, head trembling, singing every word of a shabad from memory, is the opposite of this salok's warning. Their body staggered.
So the line is less a threat than an invitation. The body's clock runs whatever we do. The mind can still choose.

how: Sikh families honor elders, who often lead the household's prayers and teach children the Gurbani they know by heart; this salok is heard at the close of every complete reading of the Guru Granth Sahib.

o: bowing the head before the Guru
the head trembling with great age
a head shaken to say no, refusing

s: the salok mocks old people for their weakness
the body isn't the problem; the problem is a mind that keeps saying later.
the salok draws great age in three short strokes
head, feet and eyes: shaking, tottering, dimming.
the salok's warning applies to people of every age
it's about the someday list, held by young and old alike.

games.q: the head shakes, the feet stagger, the eyes grow dim. what does the salok say is still missing?
o: the mind absorbed in the Lord's love.
more time to finish the list.
games.why: this is what has happened, says Nanak, and still the mind isn't absorbed in the Lord's sweetness. the warning is about the mind, not the body.

practice: Bring to mind an older person in your life, a grandparent, a neighbor, a teacher, someone in the sangat, living or gone, and picture their hands, their voice, something they taught you without meaning to.

Silently thank them, and let one way of honoring them come to mind: a call, a visit, a story asked for, or, if they've passed, one thing done the way they did it. If you pray, you can hold them before Waheguru.

wordCard.voice: Head shakes. The salok draws great age in three strokes, head, feet, eyes, and warns not about the body but about a mind that keeps saying later.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: nain, eyes. The salok says the nain have lost their light, jot.

carryVoice: Your line: turn while you can. The someday list can start with one small line. Day five hundred ninety-eight, done.

sources.ref: Salok Mahalla 9, 'sir kampio pag dagmage nain jot te heen' (Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1428)
